name: Battle of Myriokephalon
info: A Seljuk army under Sultan Kilij Arslan II ambushed the Byzantine army of Emperor Manuel I Komnenos in a mountain pass west of Iconium in 1176, ending Byzantine efforts to recover the Anatolian interior.

facts.place: The Tzivritze Pass in the mountains west of Iconium (Konya), west-central Anatolia, in present-day Turkey; the exact location is debated
facts.sides: The Byzantine Empire under Emperor Manuel I Komnenos, with Hungarian, Antiochene and Serbian contingents, estimated at 25,000 to 30,000 men by John Haldon and about 35,000 by John Birkenmeier; the Sultanate of Rum under Kilij Arslan II, whose numbers cannot be estimated, though modern historians think such a state could field at most 10,000 to 15,000 men
facts.outcome: The Byzantine army was ambushed in the pass and lost its siege train, and about half of the part engaged is thought to have become casualties. The campaign against Iconium was abandoned and a truce followed.

t: The Byzantine army was ambushed in the pass of Tzivritze, and the sultan, not the emperor, was the first to propose peace.
Estimates of the Byzantine army run from 25,000 to 30,000 men (Haldon) to about 35,000 (Birkenmeier), while no estimate of Seljuk numbers has been possible.
Byzantium won a notable victory over the Seljuks at Hyelion and Leimocheir the next year, but it was never again able to compete for dominance of the Anatolian interior.
dyk: Manuel himself compared his defeat to Manzikert, sending a message to Constantinople ahead of his army that likened his fate to that of Romanos Diogenes.
ev: A series of Byzantine campaigns against the Seljuk Turks ends in a treaty favourable to the Empire
Nur ad-Din Zangi dies, and Kilij Arslan II is free to destroy the Danishmend emirates and expel his brother Shahinshah
The peace collapses when Kilij Arslan refuses to hand over the Danishmend territory he had conquered
Manuel I gathers a large army at Lopadion and marches towards Iconium
The Seljuks ambush the Byzantine army in the Tzivritze Pass
Kilij Arslan sends the envoy Gabras to Manuel to negotiate a truce
The Byzantines defeat the Seljuks at Hyelion and Leimocheir on the Meander
Manuel concludes a probably advantageous peace with Kilij Arslan

sections.background:
Between 1158 and 1161 a series of Byzantine campaigns against the Seljuk Turks of the Sultanate of Rum ended in a treaty favourable to the Empire, with the sultan recognising a form of subordination to the emperor. Kilij Arslan II then visited Constantinople, where Manuel I Komnenos treated him as both an honoured guest and an imperial vassal. The peace was fragile. The Seljuks wanted to push from the arid central plateau of Asia Minor into the more fertile coastal lands, while the Byzantines wanted to recover the Anatolian territory lost since the Battle of Manzikert a century earlier.

During the long peace Manuel defeated Hungary and imposed Byzantine control over all the Balkans, recovered Cilicia from local Armenian dynasts and reduced the Principality of Antioch to vassal status. The peace also allowed Kilij Arslan to eliminate internal rivals and strengthen his military resources. When Nur ad-Din Zangi, the strongest Muslim ruler in Syria, died in 1174, his successor Saladin was more concerned with Egypt and Palestine than with the lands bordering the Empire. Kilij Arslan destroyed the Danishmend emirates of eastern Anatolia and ejected his brother Shahinshah, Manuel's vassal, from his lands near Ankara. Shahinshah and the Danishmend emirs fled to Byzantium. In 1175 the peace fell apart when Kilij Arslan refused to hand over a considerable proportion of the territory he had taken from the Danishmends, as the treaty obliged him to do.
sections.forces:
The Byzantine army was of exceptional size. John Haldon estimates it at 25,000 to 30,000 men, and John Birkenmeier at around 35,000, a figure derived from a supply train of 3,000 wagons, enough to support 30,000 to 40,000 men. Birkenmeier believes it held 25,000 Byzantine troops, the remainder being Hungarians sent by Manuel's kinsman Béla III of Hungary and tributary forces from the Principality of Antioch and Serbia. It was divided into divisions that entered the pass in order: a vanguard largely of infantry; the main division of eastern and western tagmata; the right wing, largely Antiochenes and other Westerners, under Baldwin of Antioch, Manuel's brother-in-law; the baggage and siege trains; the left wing under Theodore Mavrozomes and John Kantakouzenos; the emperor and his picked troops; and the rear division under the experienced general Andronikos Kontostephanos.

No estimate of Seljuk numbers for the battle has been possible. Modern historians think the successor states of the Seljuk Empire, such as the Sultanate of Rum, could field at most 10,000 to 15,000 men. The army at Dorylaeum in 1097 has been put at 6,000 to 8,000. The Seljuk force had two parts: the askars of the sultan and his emirs, full-time soldiers, often mamluks, who fought as armoured medium to heavy cavalry with bow and lance; and irregular Turkoman tribesmen, light mounted archers who served for plunder, ransom or payment and were numerous but unreliable.
sections.course:
Manuel gathered his army at Lopadion and marched towards the Seljuk border by way of Laodicea, Chonae, Lampe, Celaenae, Choma and Antioch. Kilij Arslan tried to negotiate, but Manuel, convinced of his superiority, rejected a new peace. He sent part of the army under Andronikos Vatatzes towards Amasia while his larger force marched towards Iconium. Both routes ran through heavily wooded country, and the army heading for Amasia was destroyed in an ambush. The Turks also destroyed crops and poisoned water supplies, and harassed the main army to drive it towards the pass of Tzivritze near the fortress of Myriokephalon. Manuel chose to force the pass, though the plain of Philomelion was nearby. Lack of forage and water and an outbreak of dysentery may have influenced him.

The vanguard and main division went through the pass with few casualties, and their infantry climbed the slopes to dislodge the Seljuks. The following divisions did not take this precaution, kept no closed ranks and did not use their archers well. As the rear was about to enter, the Turks closed the trap. Their attack fell especially heavily on the right wing, which lost cohesion, and Baldwin was killed. The Turks then attacked the baggage and siege trains, shooting down the draught animals and choking the road. John Kantakouzenos was slain fighting alone. A blinding dust-storm added to the confusion, and Manuel reputedly sat down passively until his officers roused him. He formed a defensive order, pushed past the wreck of the baggage and out of the pass, and joined the van and main divisions, which had built a fortified camp. Seljuk mounted archers were repulsed through the night. The next day the Turks circled the camp firing arrows, Manuel ordered two counterattacks, and there was no general action.
sections.aftermath:
Both sides suffered casualties, though their extent is difficult to quantify. Modern historians have postulated that about half of the Byzantine army was engaged and around half of those became casualties. Most importantly, Manuel's siege equipment had been captured and destroyed, and without means of attacking Iconium the Byzantines could not continue the campaign. Kilij Arslan sent an envoy named Gabras with a Nisaean warhorse and a sword to negotiate a truce. The army was to be allowed to retreat unmolested if Manuel destroyed his forts and evacuated the garrisons at Dorylaeum and Sublaeum.

Despite the sultan's protestations of good faith, Turkoman tribesmen, over whom he probably had little control, harassed the retreat. This and an earlier failure by the sultan to keep a treaty signed in 1162 gave Manuel an excuse not to observe the new terms in full. He demolished the fortifications of the less important Sublaeum but left Dorylaeum intact. He sent a message to Constantinople comparing his fate to that of Romanos Diogenes at Manzikert, yet also boasted of the treaties made beneath his own banner. A possible reason for Kilij Arslan's reluctance to renew the battle is that many of his irregulars were more interested in securing their plunder than in continuing the fight.

The next year the Byzantines won a notable victory over the Seljuks at Hyelion and Leimocheir on the Meander, where a Seljuk army blundered into an ambush laid by the general John Komnenos Vatatzes. Manuel continued to meet the Seljuks in smaller battles with some success and concluded a probably advantageous peace with Kilij Arslan in 1179.
sections.sources:
The Byzantine historian Niketas Choniates records that near the pass stood the ruins of a fortress called Myriokephalon, which gave the battle its name. He also says that Manuel considered abandoning his troops and was shamed into staying by an anonymous soldier and by Kontostephanos. A modern historian thinks this hyperbole, since flight would have put Manuel in greater danger than staying with his army. Manuel's own message to Constantinople, comparing his defeat to Manzikert while boasting of the treaties, is also reported.

Much remains uncertain. The exact location of the battle is debated among researchers. Seljuk numbers cannot be estimated, and the Byzantine figures rest on a supply train of 3,000 wagons and on estimates by Haldon and Birkenmeier. Casualties are hard to quantify. Modern historians have judged that about half the army was engaged and about half of those fell. It was reported that the Byzantine dead were scalped and mutilated, so that, as the report has it, the circumcised could not be told from the uncircumcised and the victory could be disputed. The sultan's opening of peace talks leads one historian to conclude that Kilij Arslan, though negotiating from strength, did not think his forces able to destroy the Byzantine army.
sections.legacy:
Manuel compared his defeat to Manzikert, and the battle has been called pivotal in the same way. Following it, the balance between the two powers in Anatolia gradually began to shift, and Byzantium was unable to compete for dominance of the Anatolian interior. One account holds that it was the final, unsuccessful Byzantine effort to recover the interior of Anatolia, and that after Manuel's death the empire drifted into anarchy and never again mounted a major offensive in the east. The same account holds that the Anatolian plateau was lost to the empire for ever.

Other views weigh it differently. Myriokephalon did not materially affect the capabilities of the Byzantine army, as the victory at Hyelion and Leimocheir the next year underlines, and it had more of a psychological than a military impact, proving that the Empire could not destroy Seljuk power in central Anatolia. One view is that Manuel was distracted by adventures in Italy and Egypt instead of dealing with the Turks. It has also been argued that his preoccupation with the Latins of Europe and the Crusader states was aimed at securing the Balkans and Anatolia, and that the campaign of 1176 was meant to put right the neglect of nearer matters.

Assessments of Manuel's generalship differ. He made serious tactical errors, failing to scout the route ahead effectively and ignoring the advice of his senior officers. In his defence, he organised the army in self-reliant divisions, each able to act as a small independent army, and it has been argued that this let the greater part of it survive the ambush. The failure of the infantry vanguard to sweep the Seljuks from the heights, and of the wing commanders to deploy as well as the leading divisions, is counted a major cause of the defeat.

summary: On 17 September 1176 the Seljuk Sultan Kilij Arslan II ambushed Manuel I Komnenos's Byzantine army in the Tzivritze Pass west of Iconium. Manuel's siege train was lost and the campaign ended, and Byzantium never again contested the Anatolian interior.
references: John W. Birkenmeier, The Development of the Komnenian Army: 1081–1180 (Brill, 2002)
Paul Magdalino, The Empire of Manuel I Komnenos, 1143–1180 (Cambridge University Press, 1993)
Michael Angold, The Byzantine Empire 1025–1204: A Political History (Longman, 1984)
notes: Legacy: the article's closing claims ('lost to the empire forever', 'never again in a position to mount a major offensive') sit beside its statement that the battle did not materially affect the army; both are given, attributed as views.
The scalping and mutilation report is a quotation without a named author in the article; I attributed it to a report.
Spelling variants in the article: Killij/Kilij, Nur ad-Din/Nureddin; I used Kilij and Nur ad-Din Zangi.
The article says Manuel's army 'supposedly' spread across ten miles; left out as a doubtful figure.
The article says the Anatolian lead gives Seljuk Sultan expelled brother 'Shahinshah, ruler of Ankara' while the Background says lands near Ankara; I used the latter.
Sources section is thin because the article names only Choniates; kept short on purpose.
